nodes.title: Tables 1, 2 and 3 - Qualitative information on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risk
nodes.heading: 7.1 Tables 1, 2 and 3 - Qualitative information on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risk
nodes.start_phrase: This disclosure is prepared based on the Sustainability statements in our Integrated Annual Report 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Qualitative information on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risk (Tables 1–3) within ABN AMRO’s Pillar 3 Report 2024.
- Basis of preparation: Aligned with the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024; disclosures are grounded in the outcomes of the double materiality assessment (DMA).
- Materiality approach: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), ESRS, and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER) embedded in the Enterprise Risk Management framework. In 2024, the ECB CER assessment was integrated into the ESRS DMA.
- 2024 enhancements: Strengthened ESG risk management through improved Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and updates to the risk appetite framework.
- Linkage to DMA: The 2024 CER materiality assessment informs the financial materiality dimension of the DMA.
- Time horizons: Short term = 1 year (reporting period); Medium term = 1–5 years; Long term = >5 years. Deviations are disclosed per topic.
- Scenario basis: Global base case assumes partial decarbonisation; emissions trajectory consistent with ~2.2°C warming by 2100, between IEA Announced Pledges and Stated Policies scenarios; includes chronic physical damage impacts; IFRS financial statement assumptions are aligned with this scenario.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) may reduce business productivity and damage property; near-term transition risks are expected to increase companies’ costs during the move to a low-carbon economy; additional transition impacts are anticipated.

nodes.title: Basis of preparation
nodes.heading: 7.1.1 Basis of preparation
nodes.start_phrase: This disclosure is prepared based on the Sustainability statements in our Integrated Annual Report 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Qualitative information on ESG risk (Tables 1–3), with disclosures based on the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024. The double materiality assessment (DMA) underpins the disclosures.
- Materiality approach: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER) integrated into the Enterprise Risk Management framework. In 2024, the ECB CER assessment was integrated into the ESRS assessment. Enhancements include updated Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and a strengthened risk appetite framework. 2024 CER results inform the DMA as financial materiality input.
- Time horizons: Short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), and long term (>5 years), with deviations disclosed per topic. Emphasis on forward-looking reporting for sustainability matters.

- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) can reduce business productivity and damage property; in the short term, transition risks increase costs for companies adapting to a low‑carbon economy.

nodes.title: Critical assumptions
nodes.heading: 7.1.5 Critical assumptions
nodes.start_phrase: To assess the financial impact of CER risks, we assumed that physical risk, such as floods or drought, may lead to loss of productivity for businesses and property damage for home owners.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Qualitative ESG risk disclosures (Tables 1–3), prepared from the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024, with the double materiality assessment (DMA) as the backbone.
- Materiality: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), ESRS, and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER)—with the ECB CER assessment integrated into the ESRS DMA in 2024. Enhancements include Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and updates to the risk appetite framework. CER results feed into the DMA as financial materiality input.
- Time horizons: Short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), long term (>5 years), with deviations disclosed per topic.
- Scenario basis: Global base case with partial decarbonisation progress consistent with ~2.2°C warming by 2100 (between IEA APS and STEPS), including chronic physical damage; IFRS financial statement assumptions aligned to this scenario.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) may reduce business productivity and damage properties; transition risks raise costs, may render business models obsolete or shrink demand; properties with weaker energy labels may face price declines.
- Metrics and uncertainty: Reliance on estimates, averages, and assumptions; data sourced from clients and external vendors, with sector averages used when necessary; combined data for certain metrics (e.g., financed emissions). Lower accuracy than financial metrics, especially for value chain data, due to evolving reporting, limited historical data, and non-uniform measurement practices; commitment to transparency on data and assumption changes.
- Risk definition: Sustainability risk is the potential for ESG factors to cause negative financial or non-financial impacts on the bank or society, directly or via other risk types; it is a material risk integral to the bank’s risk profile and strategy.
- Transmission channels: Microeconomic (impacts on individual clients leading to financial risks for the bank) and macroeconomic (impacts on broader economic factors that adversely affect the bank).

nodes.title: Metrics and estimation uncertainty
nodes.heading: 7.1.6 Metrics and estimation uncertainty
nodes.start_phrase: In this report we use metrics, especially in the case of our client portfolios, that are based on certain estimates, averages or assumptions.
nodes.summary:
- Transition risks can render companies’ business models obsolete, reduce product demand, and depress housing values for properties with weaker energy labels.
- Reported sustainability metrics rely on estimates, averages, assumptions, and multiple data sources (client-reported data, external vendors, sector averages), with financed emissions combining several sources.
- The accuracy of these sustainability metrics is generally lower than for financial metrics; quality varies by whether data is directly reported or proxy-based, externally reviewed, forward-looking vs. historical, and whether established frameworks exist.
- Value chain-related quantitative metrics carry high measurement uncertainty due to immature sustainability reporting among counterparties.
- Data quality and comparability are expected to improve over time as regulation standardizes disclosures, but current comparability is limited by scarce historical data and non-uniform measurement practices; different acceptable methodologies may be applied initially.
- The bank commits to transparent disclosure of changes in data and assumptions to explain movements and provide context.
- Sustainability risk is defined as the potential negative financial or non-financial impact from ESG factors on the bank or society, directly or via other risk types; it is a material risk integral to ABN AMRO’s risk management and strategy.
- ESG factors act as drivers of traditional risk types, transmitted through:
  - Microeconomic channels affecting individual clients and thus the bank’s financial risk.
  - Macroeconomic channels affecting broader economic variables (e.g., productivity, growth) that in turn impact the bank.

nodes.title: Background and definitions of sustainability risk
nodes.heading: 7.1.7 Background and definitions of sustainability risk
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability risk is defined in our risk taxonomy and sustainability risk policy as the risk that Environmental, Social or Governance-related (ESG) factors have a negative financial and/or non-financial impact on ABN AMRO or the wider society, either directly or via other risk types.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights transition risks that can render companies’ business models obsolete or depress demand, and notes potential declines in home prices for properties with weaker energy labels.
- Explains that sustainability metrics used (e.g., financed emissions) rely on estimates, averages, assumptions, and multiple data sources (client-reported data, external vendors, sector averages), leading to lower accuracy than financial metrics.
- Stresses high measurement uncertainty for value-chain data due to evolving sustainability reporting, varied data quality (direct vs proxy, reviewed vs unreviewed, forward-looking vs historical), and uneven availability of established measurement frameworks.
- Notes that data quality and comparability should improve over time with regulation and standardisation, but initial years may involve different acceptable measurement techniques; commits to transparent disclosure of data or assumption changes.
- Defines sustainability risk as ESG-related factors that can negatively affect ABN AMRO or society, directly or via traditional risk types; managing it is material to the bank’s risk profile and strategy.
- Describes transmission channels for sustainability risk:
  - Microeconomic: impacts on individual clients that translate into financial risks for the bank.
  - Macroeconomic: impacts on broader economic variables (e.g., productivity, growth) that in turn affect the bank.
- Outlines strategic focus on where impacts occur in the value chain:
  - Main downstream impact is through financed clients in lending portfolios (mortgages, corporate loans); consumer loan relevance depends on use of proceeds per EU Taxonomy.
  - Non-lending activities may be impactful but accounting methodologies are evolving; financed emissions methods for government bonds and underwriting exist, though broader guidance and approaches for undrawn facilities and guarantees remain unclear.
- States that client assets (investments managed or facilitated) are considered relevant for sustainability; influence varies by service model (discretionary, advisory, execution-only); discloses climate mitigation and workers-in-the-value-chain information.
- Acknowledges additional positive and negative impacts via products, services, and strategic choices (e.g., privacy, financial inclusion, access to services), with more detail in the Social section of the Integrated Annual Report.
- Describes a two-pronged ESG risk assessment:
  - Inside-out risks: clients’ impacts on people/planet that can create financial and non-financial risks for the bank (e.g., pollution cleanup costs).
  - Outside-in risks: climate and environmental factors affecting the bank and its clients, split into:
    - Transition risks (policy, regulation, consumer preferences, technology shifts).
    - Physical risks (acute events like floods; chronic trends like rising temperatures and biodiversity loss), with examples such as flooding affecting mortgage collateral values.

nodes.title: Strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 7.2 Strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: The main impact in our value chain is the downstream impact associated with the clients we finance, primarily through our lending portfolios — such as mortgages and corporate loans — which are central to these Sustainability Statements.
nodes.summary:
- Presents ABN AMRO’s two-pronged framework for sustainability risk: inside-out (impacts clients may have on people and planet that can create financial and non-financial risks for the bank) and outside-in (how environmental and climate factors affect the bank and its clients), spanning social, environmental effects, governance, clients, and products and services.
- Aligns sustainability with strategy and business model, emphasizing that the bank’s main sustainability impact lies downstream through financed activities, especially lending portfolios (mortgages and corporate loans). Consumer loan relevance depends on use of proceeds in line with the EU Taxonomy (e.g., real estate, renovations, motor vehicles).
- Notes that non-lending activities can be material but methodologies are evolving: financed emissions methods exist for government bonds and underwriting, yet broader guidance for government exposures and underwriting remains unclear; there is no established approach for undrawn facilities and guarantees.
- Explains the bank’s varying influence over client assets (Discretionary Portfolio Management, Advisory, Execution-only) and continues to treat them as sustainability-relevant, with disclosures on climate change mitigation and workers in the value chain.
- Acknowledges additional positive and negative impacts via products, services, and strategic choices (e.g., privacy, financial inclusion, access to services), with further detail referenced in the Social section of the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Defines risk types and gives examples: inside-out risks (e.g., client-caused pollution cleanup) and outside-in risks split into transition risks (regulatory, consumer, technology shifts during decarbonization) and physical risks (acute events like floods and chronic shifts like rising temperatures and biodiversity loss), including effects on collateral values in the mortgage portfolio.

nodes.title: Sustainability in relation to our strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 7.2.1 Sustainability in relation to our strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: The main impact in our value chain is the downstream impact associated with the clients we finance, primarily through our lending portfolios — such as mortgages and corporate loans — which are central to these Sustainability Statements.
nodes.summary:
- Explains ABN AMRO’s two-pronged approach to sustainability risk: inside-out risks (impacts clients may have on people and planet that can lead to financial and non-financial risk for the bank) and outside-in risks (how climate and environmental factors affect the bank and clients), with outside-in split into transition risk (policy, market, technology shifts) and physical risk (acute and chronic climate/environmental impacts).
- Identifies the bank’s main sustainability impacts as downstream, primarily via financed clients in lending portfolios (notably residential mortgages and corporate loans), with consumer loan relevance depending on use of proceeds aligned to EU Taxonomy.
- Notes evolving methodologies for non-lending activities: financed emissions for government bonds and underwriting exist but broader guidelines remain unclear; impacts of undrawn facilities and guarantees lack established assessment methods.
- Clarifies treatment of client assets (DPM, Advisory, Execution-only): influence varies by service, but they remain relevant for sustainability; the bank continues to disclose on climate mitigation and labor conditions in value chains.
- Links sustainability to the business model and asset mix, highlighting loans and advances as the core of total assets, predominantly mortgages and corporate loans, which drive the bank’s sustainability exposure and impact.
- Positions sustainability as a strategic pillar since 2018, operationalized via the Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS) since 2020; SAS measures “sustainability acceleration assets” bank-wide and by client unit, complements but does not replace ESRS metrics, and includes EU Taxonomy-aligned assets via the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Differentiates between volume-based SAS/GAR and impact-based climate targets (GHG reductions), acknowledging that increases in SAS may not always directly translate to immediate emission reductions; commits to improving connectivity and clarity between KPIs and impacts.
- Confirms material topics and focus areas (climate, nature, social impact) through the bank’s Double Materiality Assessment (DMA); 2024 results required no strategic changes.
- Describes governance and planning: integration of material matters into strategy and financial planning, including initiatives, risks, and opportunities; recognition that climate and environmental risks are highly likely to materialize over the medium to long term, supported by bank-wide ICAAP stress testing.
- References broader social considerations (privacy, financial inclusion, access to services) addressed in the Integrated Annual Report’s Social section.

nodes.title: Sustainability as part of our strategy
nodes.heading: 7.2.2 Sustainability as part of our strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability is a key component of ABN AMRO’s strategy, representing one of three strategic pillars.
nodes.summary:
- The document links ABN AMRO’s business model and balance sheet to sustainability, indicating which components relate, partly relate, or do not relate to sustainability matters.
- Balance sheet snapshot: total assets split into Loans and advances (65%), Financial investments (12%), and Other assets (23%); within Loans and advances, Residential mortgages (61%), Corporate loans (33%), Consumer loans (3%), and Other (3%).
- Sustainability is one of three strategic pillars, embedded since 2018 and operationalised via ambitions and targets since 2020 (ahead of CSRD).
- The Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS) is used to steer and set accountability across the bank and client units; it measures “sustainability (acceleration) assets” and includes topics deemed material in the DMA (e.g., climate change, circular economy).
- SAS is a volume-based KPI, includes EU Taxonomy-aligned assets via the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), and is designed to enable and stimulate client transition; it is not an ESRS metric nor a direct measure of progress on specific material matters.
- Complementary climate strategy metrics focus on direct impact through GHG emissions reductions; SAS growth can support climate pathways when directed to relevant sectors and mitigation purposes, but links can be indirect or time-lagged.
- Priority is to ensure KPIs are clearly tied to intended impacts and to improve connectivity across different sustainability metrics and targets while retaining metric diversity for different purposes.
- The bank’s material matters (from the DMA) are integrated into three focus areas: climate, nature, and social impact; 2024 DMA results confirmed no new or diminished material matters, so no immediate strategic changes are required.
- The financial plan outlines ongoing initiatives and associated risks and opportunities tied to these material topics.
- Climate-related and environmental risks are assessed as highly likely to materialise over the medium to long term; a bank-wide ICAAP stress test evaluated the financial impact of environmental and other risks.

nodes.title: Current and anticipated effects of material matters on strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 7.2.3 Current and anticipated effects of material matters on strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: ABN AMRO’s strategy incorporates the material matters identified in the DMA through three focus areas: climate, nature and social impact.
nodes.summary:
- The document links ABN AMRO’s business model to sustainability matters and maps business components to their sustainability relevance.
- Portfolio context: approximately 65% of total assets are loans and advances, 12% financial investments, and 23% other assets. Within the loan book, about 61% are residential mortgages, 33% corporate loans, 3% consumer loans, and 3% other.
- Sustainability is one of three strategic pillars since 2018 and has been operationalised with ambitions and targets since 2020 (ahead of CSRD).
- The Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS) is the bank’s overarching methodology to measure “sustainability (acceleration) assets” at bank and client-unit level. It incorporates DMA-identified topics (e.g., climate change, circular economy) but is not an ESRS metric; its purpose is to stimulate client transition.
- SAS (including EU Taxonomy-aligned assets via the Green Asset Ratio, GAR) is volume-based, while climate strategy metrics target direct GHG reductions. SAS growth can support climate targets but not all SAS/GAR activities have immediate or direct emission impacts. The bank aims to further connect different sustainability KPIs while keeping them purpose-fit.
- Material matters and strategy: DMA confirms three focus areas—climate, nature, and social impact—with no changes in 2024. The business model remains resilient; an ICAAP stress test over five years shows climate and environmental risks are within loss-absorbing capacity.
- Client transition approach: ABN AMRO prioritises stimulating and supporting client decarbonisation and sustainability (e.g., mortgage incentives for sustainable home improvements), while balancing environmental and social considerations and avoiding lending discrimination based on physical risk indicators.
- Environmental impacts arise mainly through financed activities (clients), covering climate change, air and water pollution, biodiversity loss, and circular economy challenges; the bank’s own operational footprint is small. ABN AMRO aims to be clients’ first-choice sustainability partner through financing and expertise.
- Social impact: focus on equality and human rights across operations and client relationships; initiatives to foster inclusivity and resilience target diverse groups (women, minorities, people with disabilities, refugees, generations, LGBTIQ+, neurodiversity), including programmes such as Reboot and B-able.
- Opportunities: the energy transition presents significant growth potential; ABN AMRO plans up to EUR 1 billion in early-stage capital by 2030 (direct equity, fund investments, hybrid debt) and aims to increase lending to renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies to EUR 10 billion by 2030.

nodes.title: Current and anticipated effects of impacts
nodes.heading: 7.2.4 Current and anticipated effects of impacts
nodes.start_phrase: ABN AMRO primarily impacts the environment through its clients.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines ABN AMRO’s assessment that its business model is resilient to adverse climate and environmental scenarios over a five-year horizon, with projected impacts remaining within its loss-absorbing capacity. The bank’s strategy centers on supporting clients’ sustainability transitions—e.g., offering mortgage incentives for sustainable home upgrades—while balancing environmental goals with social responsibilities such as enabling home ownership, and it does not discriminate in lending based on physical risk indicators. It emphasizes that the bank’s environmental impacts arise primarily through financed activities (climate change, air and water pollution, biodiversity loss, circularity challenges), with limited direct operational footprint, and commits to aligning operations and client engagement with climate and environmental objectives. On social impact, ABN AMRO focuses on equality and human rights, acknowledging both positive and negative effects, and advances inclusivity through initiatives targeting diverse groups, including neurodiversity and programs like Reboot and B‑able. The Double Materiality Assessment identifies climate-related opportunities: up to EUR 1 billion by 2030 for early-stage transition capital (via equity, funds, hybrid debt) and expanding lending to renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies to EUR 10 billion by 2030. References are made to further details in the Integrated Annual Report 2024 (Business risk and Social sections) and the Pillar 3 Report 2024.

nodes.title: Risk management of sustainability matters
nodes.heading: 7.3 Risk management of sustainability matters
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability risks, including the risk of negative impacts, that relate to our clients are managed in line with the bank’s enterprise risk management cycle (ERM cycle), also referred to as the Sustainability Risk Management Framework.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ABN AMRO’s sustainability risk management for client-related risks within its Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) cycle, termed the Sustainability Risk Management Framework.
- Scope: Applies to all clients across their lifecycle—from onboarding and due diligence to potential exit—covering downstream value chain impacts and negative externalities.
- Framework elements: Integration of sustainability risks into business strategy and decision-making; risk identification and materiality; assessment and measurement; risk appetite; control and monitoring; reporting; and risk response.
- Tools and processes: Climate, environmental and social risk heatmaps; CER materiality assessment; portfolio scenario analysis; CASY (Client Assessment on SustainabilitY); stress testing; lending criteria; risk policies; client engagement; target-setting and climate strategy; sustainability risk reporting to business, risk, and executive committees.
- Governance: Multi-layered risk governance with dedicated sub-committees:
  - Business Risk Committees (BRCs): Unit-level oversight of sustainability risks and approvals, including scenario analysis (monthly/quarterly).
  - Scenario and Stress-test Committee (SSC): Oversees climate and environmental risk scenarios and stress tests (quarterly).
  - Financial Crime Risk Committee (FCRC): Bank-wide decisions on financial crime risks (AML, CTF, sanctions, bribery, corruption, tax integrity, fraud) with sustainability linkages such as environmental crime proceeds (monthly).
  - Methodology Acceptance Group (MAG): Validates and approves risk and climate stress-testing models (monthly).
  - Impairment & Provisioning Committee (IPC): Manages impairments and provisions, including climate transition risk-related credit losses (monthly).
- Execution: Day-to-day oversight by the Sustainability Risk team within Central Risk Management.
- First line support: Engagement Committee (executive business-led) oversees client and sector engagement activities aligned with sustainability risk objectives.

nodes.title: Sustainability risk management framework relating to ABN AMROs clients
nodes.heading: 7.3.1 Sustainability risk management framework relating to ABN AMROs clients
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability risks, including the risk of negative impacts, that relate to our clients are managed in line with the bank’s enterprise risk management cycle (ERM cycle), also referred to as the Sustainability Risk Management Framework.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines ABN AMRO’s Sustainability Risk Management Framework for client-related sustainability risks, aligned with the bank’s enterprise risk management (ERM) cycle and applied across the full client lifecycle from onboarding and due diligence to potential exit.
- Explains that the framework operationalises governance and policy to manage risks and negative impacts in the downstream value chain, embedding sustainability risk into business strategy, decision-making, identification/materiality, assessment/measurement, control/monitoring, reporting, and response.
- Lists key tools and processes used, including climate, environmental and social risk heatmaps; materiality assessments; portfolio scenario analysis; CASY (Client Assessment on SustainabilitY); stress testing; lending criteria; risk policies; engagement; risk appetite setting; and sustainability risk reporting to business, risk, and executive committees.
- Describes the sustainability risk governance structure via risk management sub-committees:
  - Business Risk Committees (BRCs): unit-level oversight and approvals on sustainability risk topics (e.g., scenario analysis); meet monthly/quarterly.
  - Scenario and Stress-test Committee (SSC): oversees climate and environmental risk scenarios and stress testing; meets quarterly.
  - Financial Crime Risk Committee (FCRC): bank-wide decisions on financial crime risks (ML/TF, sanctions, bribery, corruption, tax integrity, fraud), including sustainability-related aspects like proceeds of environmental crime; meets monthly.
  - Methodology Acceptance Group (MAG): validates and approves risk and other models, including climate stress testing methodologies; meets monthly.
  - Impairment & Provisioning Committee (IPC): manages impairments/provisions and may address sustainability-linked credit losses (e.g., climate transition risk); meets monthly.
- Notes day-to-day oversight by the Sustainability Risk team within Central Risk Management.
- Highlights first line of defence support via executive business-led committees such as the Engagement Committee, mandated by the Executive Board to oversee client and sector engagement activities.

nodes.title: Sustainability risk governance relating to ABN AMRO’s clients
nodes.heading: 7.3.2 Sustainability risk governance relating to ABN AMRO’s clients
nodes.start_phrase: Risk management sub-committees (positioned directly below the Board-level executive committees) support effective and efficient risk management throughout the bank, each with their own remit:
nodes.summary:
- ABN AMRO applies a Sustainability Risk Management Framework aligned with its enterprise risk management (ERM) cycle to manage sustainability risks, including negative impacts, related to clients across their full lifecycle (onboarding, ongoing due diligence, potential exit).
- The framework operationalises risk governance and the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework for downstream value chain risks and is supported by tools such as climate/environmental/social risk heatmaps, materiality assessments, portfolio scenario analysis, CASY (Client Assessment on SustainabilitY), stress testing, lending criteria, engagement, risk appetite setting, and sustainability risk reporting to business, risk and executive committees.
- Governance is executed through risk sub-committees beneath Board-level executive committees:
  - Business Risk Committees (oversight of sustainability risk in client units; approve unit-specific issues; monthly/quarterly).
  - Scenario and Stress-test Committee (oversight of climate/environmental risks, scenarios and stress tests; quarterly).
  - Financial Crime Risk Committee (bank-wide decisions on financial crime risks, including sustainability aspects like proceeds of environmental crime; monthly).
  - Methodology Acceptance Group (validates risk and climate stress testing models; monthly).
  - Impairment & Provisioning Committee (manages impairments/provisions, including climate transition-related credit losses; monthly).
- Day-to-day oversight is performed by the Sustainability Risk team within Central Risk Management. The first-line Engagement Committee oversees client, sector and material supplier engagements on ESG risk, ensuring documentation and alignment with bank policies, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and OECD Guidelines.
- The Sustainability Risk Policy Framework comprises the Sustainability Risk Policy, Standards and Exclusions, reviewed annually to reflect new insights, stakeholder views and regulatory guidance (ECB/EBA). Exclusions include an Exclusion List and a Controversial Weapons List.
- Standards referenced include the Sustainability Acceleration Standard, Sustainability Risk Standard for Defence, Sustainability Risk Standard for Project Finance, and a Sustainability Risk Standard with Client Requirements, supported by a Risk Taxonomy.
- The Sustainability Risk Policy sets principles and minimum requirements for managing client-related sustainability risks, covering definitions, governance, engagement with non-compliant clients, and controls across client onboarding, lifecycle management, lending and proprietary investments. It is approved by the Group Risk Committee under delegated authority from the Executive Board, reviewed at least annually with internal and external stakeholder input, and communicated across the first and second lines of defence, with a public abbreviated version available.

nodes.title: Sustainability risk policy framework
nodes.heading: 7.3.3 Sustainability risk policy framework
nodes.start_phrase: Our Sustainability Risk Policy Framework underpins how the bank manages sustainability risk, including negative impacts, in relation to our clients.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the bank’s approach to ESG risk engagement with clients and material suppliers, ensuring documentation and measures align with the bank’s ESG risk appetite and with UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs) and OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.
- Outlines the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework, which includes the policy, standards, and exclusions; is reviewed annually; and is aligned with evolving regulatory guidance (ECB/EBA), internal/external developments, and stakeholder input.
- Details exclusions: the bank will not knowingly provide products or services on its Exclusion List or do business with clients on its Controversial Weapons List, as referenced in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Presents the Sustainability Governance Structure, comprising:
  - Sustainability Risk Policy (SRP)
  - Standards: Sustainability Acceleration Standard; Sustainability Risk Standard for Defence; Sustainability Risk Standard for Project Finance; Sustainability Risk Standard with Client Requirements
  - Exclusions: Exclusion List; Controversial Weapons List
  - Risk Taxonomy
- Explains the sustainability risk policy’s scope and requirements:
  - Defines sustainability risks and governance arrangements
  - Sets minimum requirements for managing sustainability risks across the client lifecycle (onboarding, ongoing due diligence, potential exit), lending activities, and proprietary investments
  - Describes how the bank engages with clients that do not meet standards
- Governance and approval: the Group Risk Committee (under Executive Board delegation) approves the policy; it is reviewed and approved at least annually with input from internal units (e.g., Credit Risk, client units) and external stakeholders (e.g., NGOs); communicated to first and second lines of defence; and summarized publicly on the bank’s website.

nodes.title: Sustainability-related standards and generic principles applicable to corporate clients
nodes.heading: 7.3.4 Sustainability-related standards and generic principles applicable to corporate clients
nodes.start_phrase: Our Standards and Generic Principles define the sustainability requirements against which our corporate clients must be assessed to ensure appropriate risk response measures.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines a bank’s sustainability-related standards and generic principles that underpin its Sustainability Risk Policy Framework (SRPF) for assessing corporate clients, especially in higher-risk sectors. Core client expectations include legal compliance and transparency; identification and mitigation of salient human rights risks; a satisfactory ESG track record; meaningful stakeholder engagement and grievance handling; promotion of circularity and reduced virgin material use; monitoring and reduction of GHG emissions in line with the Paris Agreement; awareness of and action to preserve ecosystem services; preparedness for the Net Zero transition; management of impacts on biodiversity, water, air, and soil; and mitigation of physical climate risks.

These Generic Principles are the foundation of ESG assessments for all corporate financing and are operationalised across Corporate Banking, Wealth Management, and Personal & Business Banking. They support alignment with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, and address EU Taxonomy Article 18. The underlying Standard with Client Requirements has been enhanced for consistent application across clients, aligned with CSRD/ESRS terminology, and calibrated to client maturity by size and sector. Sectoral updates include: (1) expanded exclusion of direct lending to oil and gas fields licensed for development after 2023, in line with the IEA Net Zero 2050 scenario; and (2) removal of the exclusion on stand-alone project finance for nuclear power, coupled with strengthened due diligence and stringent financing criteria. The text also situates these requirements within the bank’s Sustainability Risk Management Framework and ERM cycle, where strategy is set by the first line of defence and oversight is provided by the second line.

nodes.title: Business strategy and strategic decision-making (steps 1 and 7)
nodes.heading: 7.3.5 Business strategy and strategic decision-making (steps 1 and 7)
nodes.start_phrase: The Sustainability Risk Management Framework, which operationalises how we manage sustainability matters via the ERM cycle, starts with the setting of the business strategy by the first line of defence.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines generic sustainability principles and minimum requirements for corporate clients, especially in higher-risk sectors, under the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework (SRPF).
- Client expectations include legal compliance, transparent responsible conduct, human rights due diligence and grievance handling, satisfactory ESG track record, stakeholder engagement, circularity and waste reduction, GHG monitoring and Paris-aligned reductions, safeguarding ecosystem services, preparation for Net Zero transition, protection of biodiversity, water, air and soil, and mitigation of physical climate risks.
- These principles form the foundation of ESG assessments across Corporate Banking, Wealth Management, and Personal & Business Banking, and support compliance with UNGPs, OECD MNE Guidelines, and EU Taxonomy Article 18.
- The Standard with Client Requirements has been enhanced to apply consistently across all clients, align with CSRD/ESRS terminology, and account for client maturity by size/sector.
- Energy sector policy updates: expanded exclusion of direct lending to oil and gas fields licensed for development after 2023 (aligned with IEA NZE 2050), and removal of the blanket exclusion for stand-alone project finance for nuclear power, paired with strengthened due diligence and strict financing criteria.
- Describes integration of sustainability into business strategy via the Sustainability Risk Management Framework and ERM cycle: first line sets strategy; second line provides risk oversight and control.
- Strategic decisions (client engagement, portfolio adjustments, climate strategy) are informed by sustainability risk insights; risk appetite limits reflect strategic sustainability commitments (e.g., carbon reduction), and KPIs/KRIs are considered together.
- Explains risk identification and materiality processes using Environmental and Social Risk heatmaps, quarterly emerging risk scans, and the Risk Event Register feeding the risk taxonomy and scenarios.
- Heatmaps assess sub-sectors’ inherent sensitivities across corporate lending and residential real estate, using sectoral (64 sub-sectors) and geographic lenses, and over 40 underlying physical, transition, and negative impact events.
- Aggregated heatmap scoring uses the most sensitive (conservative) factor among negative impact, transition risk, and physical risk to guide materiality, stress testing, and risk appetite.

nodes.title: Risk identification and materiality assessment (step 2)
nodes.heading: 7.3.6 Risk identification and materiality assessment (step 2)
nodes.start_phrase: The risk identification part of the ERM cycle relies to a large extent on our Environmental and Social Risk heatmaps.
nodes.summary:
- The document describes how the bank’s sustainability strategy is integrated with its enterprise risk management (ERM) cycle and aligned with risk appetite and second line risk policies, creating a two-way linkage: sustainability risk insights guide strategic choices (client engagement, portfolio steering), while strategic commitments (e.g., carbon reduction targets) shape risk appetite limits and policy updates; KPIs and KRIs are considered together.
- Risk identification and materiality (ERM step 2) rely on Environmental & Social Risk heatmaps and quarterly emerging risk scans; the most material emerging risks feed the Risk Event Register, which informs the risk taxonomy and scenario booklet.
- The heatmaps assess inherent sensitivity to sustainability events across 64 corporate sub-sectors and relevant geographies in corporate lending (downstream value chain) and residential real estate, covering over 40 physical, transition, and negative impact events (e.g., flooding, water stress, policy/market effects, GHG emissions, water use intensity).
- Sensitivities are aggregated conservatively by taking the most sensitive factor per topic and presented across topics E1–E5 (climate change, pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity/ecosystems, circular economy) and S2–S3 (workers in the value chain, affected communities); E3 and S3 were included in identification but assessed non-material in subsequent double materiality.
- Risk assessment and measurement (ERM step 3) occur at multiple levels:
  - Bank level: climate and environmental risks are embedded in internal stress testing.
  - Portfolio level: scenario analyses (in 2024 for residential and commercial real estate) and product approval/review processes incorporate sustainability risks.
  - Client level: three tools are used—CASY (for corporate clients with lending > EUR 1 million) to check compliance with the Sustainability Risk Framework; TRA to gauge transition readiness in climate-strategy sectors; and RCT to classify vulnerability to climate and environmental risks. CASY and RCT outputs feed credit assessment, second-line validation, and decisions.
- In 2024, the CASY tool was enhanced to strengthen sector-specific ESG risk assessment against Generic Principles, with tailored requirements for higher-risk sectors; sectors are assigned risk levels across six ESG themes, enabling more granular, better-informed client evaluations where social and environmental/climate risks may differ by sector.

nodes.title: Risk assessment and measurement (step 3)
nodes.heading: 7.3.7 Risk assessment and measurement (step 3)
nodes.start_phrase: Various tools are used to assess and measure sustainability risk at different levels:
nodes.summary:
- Presents environmental and social risk heatmaps for corporate loans across ESG topics: climate change (E1), pollution (E2), water and marine resources (E3), biodiversity and ecosystems (E4), circular economy (E5), workers in the value chain (S2) and affected communities (S3). The heatmaps distribute sensitivity from low to high and enable cross-topic comparison. For E1–E4, both transition and physical risks are considered; for E5, S2 and S3, sensitivity to negative impacts related to transition risks is considered. E3 and S3 were identified but later assessed as non-material in the double materiality assessment.

- Details the risk assessment and measurement approach (step 3) at three levels:
  - Bank level: climate and environmental risks embedded in internal stress tests and scenarios.
  - Portfolio level: scenario analysis to measure sustainability risk; 2024 climate scenario analyses conducted for residential and commercial real estate; product approval/review processes integrate sustainability risks (e.g., mortgages).
  - Client level: three tools used and integrated into credit risk assessment, second-line validation and decisions:
    - Client Assessment on Sustainability (CASY) for lending > EUR 1 million, aligned to the Sustainability Risk Framework.
    - Transition Readiness Assessment (TRA) for sectors/clients in scope of the climate strategy.
    - Climate and Environmental Risk Classification Tool (RCT) for non-programme corporate lending, classifying vulnerability to climate/environmental risks.

- Explains 2024 enhancements to CASY:
  - Strengthened sector-specific view and client performance assessment against typical ESG risks (climate impact, biodiversity, human rights, workers in value chains).
  - Sectors assigned risk levels across six ESG themes; clients expected to have mitigants, policies and measures commensurate with risk level.
  - Engagement considered if client performance is not aligned with expectations.
  - Early assessment against Generic Principles started in 2024; broader rollout of the upgraded tool planned for 2025, including lower ESG-risk sectors.

- Sets out risk response (step 4):
  - Bank-level mitigations: exclusion list (e.g., illegal logging), Controversial Weapons List, strict sector requirements under the Sustainability Risk Standard, integration of sustainability risk in credit and business risk policies, and a climate strategy for high-emission sectors.
  - Client/portfolio-level mitigations via engagement with three categories:
    - Normal intensity: tailored, ongoing remediation of policy breaches.
    - High intensity: formal, time-bound objectives with close monitoring and quarterly oversight by the Engagement Committee.
    - Thematic: sector-wide engagements to address emerging or systemic ESG risks and advance strategic sustainability goals; example in 2024: shipping sector.

- Covers risk control, monitoring and reporting (steps 5 and 6):
  - Top-down monitoring against the Strategic Risk Appetite Statement (SRAS), which includes managing portfolios on a net zero by 2050 trajectory.
  - The SRAS informs the Bank Risk Appetite Statement (BRAS).
  - Sustainability risk appetite set beneath the BRAS with indicators capturing inside-out and outside-in perspectives; limits and checkpoints applied at bank-wide, client unit and function levels to trigger timely mitigation.
  - Indicators are continuously refined as more granular data becomes available.

nodes.title: Risk response (step 4)
nodes.heading: 7.3.8 Risk response (step 4)
nodes.start_phrase: To ensure that sustainability risk is managed in line with the bank’s risk appetite and strategy, mitigating actions are defined at bank, portfolio and client levels.
nodes.summary:
- Sets expectations for corporate clients to have risk mitigants, policies, and measures proportionate to their assigned ESG risk level, with higher performance expected where risks are high; non‑alignment may trigger engagement.
- Describes migration to a new CASY assessment approach: in 2024, applying Generic Principles to higher-ESG-sensitivity sectors across climate, biodiversity, human rights, and value-chain labor; in 2025, extending to lower-risk sectors.
- Outlines Risk Response (step 4) across bank, portfolio, and client levels:
  - Bank-level mitigations: exclusion list (e.g., illegal logging), Controversial Weapons List, strict lending requirements via the Sustainability Risk Standard with Sector Requirements, integration of sustainability risks into credit/business risk policies, and a climate strategy focused on high-emission sectors and portfolios.
  - Client/portfolio-level mitigations: structured engagements with financed clients that do not meet standards, categorized as:
    - Normal intensity: tailored, ongoing remediation of policy breaches.
    - High intensity: formal, time-bound objectives with close monitoring and quarterly Engagement Committee oversight.
    - Thematic: sector-wide engagements when industries risk breaching ESG/human rights requirements; used for risk mitigation and strategic acceleration (e.g., 2024 engagement in the shipping sector).
- Details Risk Control & Monitoring and Reporting (steps 5 and 6):
  - Top-down monitoring against the Strategic Risk Appetite Statement (SRAS), covering sustainable business model & value creation (including net-zero 2050 alignment), financial soundness, and sound operating environment; SRAS informs the Bank Risk Appetite Statement (BRAS).
  - Establishes a sustainability risk appetite beneath BRAS using indicators that capture key ESG factors and both inside-out and outside-in risk perspectives, with limits/checkpoints monitored at bank-wide, client-unit, and function levels; indicators are refined as data quality and granularity improve.

nodes.title: Risk control & monitoring and risk reporting (steps 5 and 6)
nodes.heading: 7.3.9 Risk control & monitoring and risk reporting (steps 5 and 6)
nodes.start_phrase: Monitoring activities aim to act as a safety net to capture and identify potential shortcomings in our Sustainability Risk Policy Framework in a timely manner.
nodes.summary:
- ESG risk assessment approach: Clients are expected to have mitigants and policies aligned with their assigned ESG risk level; higher-risk clients are expected to perform better. ABN AMRO began assessing clients in 2024 using Generic Principles ahead of a 2025 CASY update, prioritizing sectors with higher ESG sensitivity (climate, biodiversity, human rights, value-chain labor), with rollout to lower-risk sectors planned for 2025.
- Risk response framework (step 4): Mitigating actions defined at bank, portfolio, and client levels to align sustainability risk with risk appetite and strategy.
- Bank-level mitigants: Sector and sub-sector exclusions (e.g., illegal logging) via the Exclusion List; a Controversial Weapons List prohibiting any relationship with involved firms; strict corporate lending requirements under the Sustainability Risk Standard with Sector Requirements; embedding sustainability risk in credit and business risk policies; climate strategy targeting high-emission sectors and portfolio management.
- Client/portfolio-level action: Engagement with non-compliant clients to improve performance, using three engagement types:
  - Normal intensity: tailored, ongoing remediation of policy breaches.
  - High intensity: formal, time-bound objectives, closely monitored, quarterly oversight by an Engagement Committee.
  - Thematic: sector-wide engagements when industries risk breaching ESG (including human rights) requirements; used for risk mitigation and to advance strategic sustainability goals. Example: 2024 thematic engagement in the shipping sector.
- Risk control, monitoring, and reporting (steps 5–6): Monitoring to detect framework shortcomings; top-down measurement of the bank’s risk profile against the Strategic Risk Appetite Statement (SRAS) covering sustainable business model & value creation, financial soundness, and operating environment, including managing portfolios toward a net-zero 2050 trajectory. SRAS informs the Bank Risk Appetite Statement (BRAS).
- Sustainability risk appetite: Indicators set below BRAS capture key ESG factors from both inside-out and outside-in perspectives, with limits and checkpoints monitored at bank-wide, client unit, and function levels; indicators are refined as data improves. Additional KRIs are set at unit/function level and are increasingly informed by scenario analyses. In 2024, internal monitoring and testing controls were strengthened, especially for client onboarding, review, and lending processes.
- Risk appetite indicators include: percentage of clients needing valid ESG risk assessments; Sustainable & Acceleration Standard volume change; EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio; changes in portfolio carbon footprints; progress toward NZBA targets; climate strategy sector performance; relative exposure to sectors sensitive to physical and transition environmental risks; strength of human rights risk management; and exposure to sectors sensitive to social risk.
- Governance and reporting cadence: Adherence status and outlook reviewed monthly by the Executive Board and quarterly by the Supervisory Board via the Enterprise Risk Management report (EU OVA).
- Climate & Environmental Risks (CER) materiality assessment: Conducted annually across traditional banking risk types as part of ERM; feeds risk taxonomy and the bank’s double materiality assessment. Scope covers the entire balance sheet: credit risk assessment of the loan book; market and liquidity risk assessments stress fair value assets for CER; non-financial risk covers property and equipment. Results are presented for short-, medium-, and long-term horizons.

nodes.title: Sustainability risk appetite indicators
nodes.heading: 7.3.10 Sustainability risk appetite indicators
nodes.start_phrase: The status of adherence to the risk appetite and the outlook are discussed monthly by the Executive Board and quarterly by the Supervisory Board, based on the Enterprise Risk Management report, as stated under EU OVA.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes risk appetite limits and checkpoints at bank-wide, client unit, and function levels to strengthen sustainability risk monitoring.
- Expands key risk indicators (KRIs) at client unit/function level, increasingly informed by sustainability risk identification and scenario analyses.
- In 2024, enhances adherence to the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework via added internal monitoring and testing controls, with a focus on client onboarding, client reviews, and lending processes.
- Defines sustainability risk appetite indicators across:
  - Sustainability risk: percentage of clients requiring valid ESG risk assessments; Sustainable and Acceleration Standard volume change; Green Asset Ratio (EU Taxonomy-aligned volume).
  - Climate risk: change in portfolio carbon footprint; coverage of Net Zero Banking Alliance decarbonisation commitments; climate strategy sector performance.
  - Environmental risk: relative exposure to sectors sensitive to physical and transition environmental risks.
  - Human rights risk: strength of human rights risk management; exposure to sectors sensitive to social risk.
- Distinguishes between indicators with checkpoints/limits and those used for monitoring only.
- Governance: Executive Board reviews adherence and outlook monthly; Supervisory Board reviews quarterly via the Enterprise Risk Management report (per EU OVA).
- Conducts an annual Climate & Environmental Risks (CER) materiality assessment within the ERM cycle for traditional banking risk types, feeding into the bank’s risk taxonomy and double materiality assessment.
- CER scope covers the entire balance sheet:
  - Credit risk: loan book assessment.
  - Market and liquidity risk: stress of fair-valued assets for CER.
  - Non-financial risk: property and equipment impacts.
- Presents 2024 CER assessment results across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, with further risk-type details provided elsewhere in the report.

nodes.title: CER materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 7.3.11 CER materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: A materiality assessment on Climate & Environmental Risks (CER) is carried out annually for traditional banking risk types.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes a multi-level sustainability risk governance and monitoring setup, with risk appetite limits and checkpoints at bank-wide, client unit, and functional levels, and expanded KRIs embedded within client units/functions informed by scenario analyses.
- Introduces in 2024 additional internal monitoring and testing controls to ensure adherence to the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework, with emphasis on client onboarding, review, and lending processes.
- Defines sustainability risk appetite indicators across:
  - Sustainability risk: percentage of clients with valid ESG assessments, Sustainable & Acceleration Standard volume change, Green Asset Ratio (EU Taxonomy-aligned).
  - Climate risk: carbon footprint change in lending/investment portfolios, coverage of NZBA decarbonisation commitments, sector performance vs climate strategy.
  - Environmental risk: relative exposure to sectors sensitive to physical and transition environmental risks.
  - Human rights risk: strength of risk management and exposure to sectors sensitive to social risk.
- Sets oversight cadence: Executive Board reviews monthly and Supervisory Board quarterly via the Enterprise Risk Management report (EU OVA).
- Conducts an annual Climate & Environmental Risk (CER) materiality assessment across the full balance sheet, informing the bank’s risk taxonomy and double materiality assessment; evaluates credit, market (trading and banking book), liquidity, business, and non-financial risks over short-, medium-, and long-term horizons.
- Credit risk deep dive:
  - Scope covers ~90% of lending (mortgages, commercial real estate, corporate); excludes Clearing clients and consumer loans.
  - Methodology applies expected loss approaches for physical risks (event probability, loss severity, collateral LTV effects) and transition risks (NGFS, carbon pricing scenarios).
  - Findings: environmental risk impact on credit risk is material in short, medium, and long term; climate risk material for credit risk predominantly over longer horizons.
  - Measurement tools include climate risk heatmaps, mortgage/CRE scenario analyses, corporate portfolio stress tests, and environmental risk scenarios; environmental risk materiality primarily qualitative supported by scenarios.
- Mitigation measures span credit acceptance standards, enhanced monitoring, risk appetite setting (including limits/checkpoints for vulnerable collateral in higher physical risk areas in mortgages and monitoring carbon-related corporate exposures), and financial buffers.
- Capitalisation and provisioning approach:
  - Uses IFRS 9 ECL with macroeconomic scenarios that implicitly incorporate CER.
  - Ongoing integration of CER into credit risk models; currently applies management overlays for climate and environmental transition risks and an economic capital add-on for climate transition risk.
  - Concludes provisioning is adequate given scenarios and overlays.

nodes.title: CER materiality assessment - Credit risk
nodes.heading: 7.3.12 CER materiality assessment - Credit risk
nodes.start_phrase: In scope of the CER materiality assessment in Credit risk are the mortgages, commercial real estate (CRE) and corporate portfolios as these are the main portfolios for which clear transmission channels are determined.
nodes.summary:
- The document presents a materiality assessment framework for climate and environmental risk (CER), distinguishing physical and transition risks across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons and mapping potential materiality across key risk types: credit risk, market risk (trading and banking books), liquidity risk, business risk, and non-financial risk.
- Focus on CER materiality for Credit Risk:
  - Scope: mortgages, commercial real estate (CRE), and corporate portfolios, covering ~90% of the lending book; clearing clients and consumer loans are out of scope.
  - Approach: product-based assessment for real-estate–collateralised loans (residential mortgages, CRE) and corporate loans where clear transmission channels exist.
  - Methodology:
    - Physical risk: expected loss approach combining event probability, loss severity, and effects on collateral loan-to-value.
    - Transition risk: similar expected loss approach using scenario analyses, including NGFS pathways and carbon pricing.
  - Findings (2024): environmental risk impact on credit risk is material in the short, medium, and long term; climate risk is also material, particularly over the longer term.
- Identification and measurement tools include a climate risk heatmap, scenario analyses for mortgage and CRE portfolios, a climate stress test for part of the corporate portfolio, and an environmental risk scenario analysis; environmental risk materiality relies mainly on qualitative assessment supported by scenarios.
- Mitigating measures span credit risk acceptance, risk monitoring, risk appetite setting, and financial buffers.
- Risk appetite: climate physical and transition risk indicators were added to the 2024 Risk Appetite Statement; limits and checkpoints are set for vulnerable collateral in higher physical-risk areas within mortgages, and carbon-related exposures are monitored in the corporate lending portfolio; this remains a developing area.
- Capitalisation and provisioning: IFRS 9 Expected Credit Loss (ECL) models use macroeconomic scenarios that implicitly include CER; full CER integration into credit risk models is in progress. Interim measures include management overlays for climate and environmental transition risks and an economic capital add-on for climate transition risk. Combined with macro scenarios, the bank considers provisioning for CER adequate.

nodes.title: Climate and Environmental Risk in the Credit Risk Model Landscape
nodes.heading: 7.3.13 Climate and Environmental Risk in the Credit Risk Model Landscape
nodes.start_phrase: Incorporating CER into the credit risk model landscape is challenging for multiple reasons.
nodes.summary:
- Objective: Integrate climate and environmental risk (CER) into the credit risk model landscape despite data gaps, evolving regulation, limited historical evidence, and horizon uncertainty.
- Roadmap: Embed CER across the credit risk framework from loan origination (to build granular future data) through modelling, stress testing, and reporting for PD/LGD models, capital adequacy (economic capital and Basel IRB), and IFRS 9.
- Market risk (trading book): CER assessed as immaterial; stress scenarios on market risk factors show limited P&L impact due to concentration in sovereign and highly rated financial bonds with low sensitivity to physical/transition risks.
- Market risk (banking book): CER impact on net interest income deemed immaterial; scenario analysis indicates low effect because portfolios most exposed to CER have relatively low interest-rate sensitivity.
- Liquidity risk: Quantitative short- and medium-term assessment found CER impact not currently material. Review covered potential net cash outflows, liquidity buffer depletion, funding market access/costs, and liquidity value under both physical and transition risks. Active funding plan management and sustainability initiatives support immateriality; longer-term effects are managed via business steering (with potential P&L impacts classified as business risk).
- Business risk: Assessed using qualitative and expert judgment plus existing quantitative work (ECB 2022 Climate Stress Test, environmental risk heatmap, climate scenarios). Transition risk evaluated via effects of CO2 reduction targets on lending volumes and revenues across sectors and time horizons.

nodes.title: CER materiality assessment - Market risk in the trading book
nodes.heading: 7.3.14 CER materiality assessment - Market risk in the trading book
nodes.start_phrase: Climate and environmental risk events can materialise in market risks within the trading book.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines how ABN AMRO is integrating Climate and Environmental Risk (CER) into its credit risk model landscape, noting key challenges such as limited granular/high-quality data, evolving regulation, and scarce historical CER impacts, which create uncertainty across time horizons.
- It presents a roadmap that spans the credit risk lifecycle: building future granular data at loan origination; incorporating CER into modelling and stress testing for PD and LGD; and reflecting impacts in capital adequacy reporting (economic capital, Basel IRB) and IFRS 9.
- CER materiality assessments across risk types conclude:
  - Market risk (trading book): Scenario shocks to market risk factors (e.g., credit spreads) show immaterial impact, given concentration in sovereigns and highly rated financials with low sensitivity to physical and transition risks.
  - Market risk (banking book): Potential CER effects on net interest income via client behavior, regulation, yield curve changes, and funding spreads are assessed as low/immaterial due to low interest rate sensitivity in portfolios most exposed to CER.
  - Liquidity risk: A 2024 quantitative assessment (short term within 1 year, medium term within 5 years) considers predefined physical and transition events, impacts on net cash outflows, liquidity buffer depletion, funding market access/costs, and buffer liquidity value. Frequent funding plan updates and sustainability initiatives support the conclusion that CER impact on liquidity is not currently material; longer-term effects can be managed through business steering (with any P&L impact captured under business risk).
  - Business risk: Evaluated using qualitative and expert judgment combined with existing quantitative work (2022 ECB Climate Stress Test, ABN AMRO’s environmental risk heatmap, climate scenario analyses). Transition risk is assessed via the effect of CO2 reduction targets on lending volumes and revenues across sectors and time horizons.

nodes.title: CER materiality assessment - Market risk in the banking book
nodes.heading: 7.3.15 CER materiality assessment - Market risk in the banking book
nodes.start_phrase: Climate and environmental risk (CER) events can materialise in market risks within the banking book.
nodes.summary:
- Integrating climate and environmental risk (CER) into the credit risk model landscape, outlining key challenges—limited granular/high-quality data, evolving regulations, limited historical CER impacts on credit risk, and uncertainty across time horizons—and a roadmap from loan origination data capture to modeling, stress testing, PD/LGD models, and capital/IFRS 9 reporting.

nodes.title: CER materiality assessment - Business risk
nodes.heading: 7.3.17 CER materiality assessment - Business risk
nodes.start_phrase: The CER business risk relates to the present and potential effect of events on the operating result of the bank.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and challenge: Describes integrating Climate and Environmental Risk (CER) into ABN AMRO’s credit risk framework amid data gaps, evolving regulation, limited historical loss evidence, and long, uncertain horizons. Outlines a roadmap from loan origination and data capture to PD/LGD modeling, stress testing, and capital/IFRS 9 reporting.

- Market risk (trading book): Stressing market risk factors (e.g., credit spreads) shows immaterial CER impact due to concentration in sovereign and highly rated financial bonds with low sensitivity to physical and transition risks.

- Market risk (banking book): Scenario analysis of CER effects on net interest income via client behavior, regulation, curves, and funding spreads indicates low sensitivity; assessed immaterial.

- Liquidity risk: Quantitative short- and medium-term assessment finds CER impact on net cash outflows, funding access/costs, and buffer value not currently material, supported by frequent funding plan updates and sustainability initiatives.

- Business risk: Assessed using expert judgment and existing analyses (ECB Climate Stress Test 2022, risk heatmap, scenario analyses). Transition risk tied to CO2 targets may affect lending volumes/revenues; not material short term but potentially material medium/long term. Risk mitigation via expanding sector targets and portfolio steering.

- Physical risk: No historical material impact on operating expenses; expected to build over time, notably in mortgages and commercial real estate through collateral damage (flooding, foundation issues). Single-event income impact currently marginal.

- Environmental risk: Arises from environmental degradation and transition dynamics; high-probability, potentially material drivers include regulation and technology. Managed through long-term strategic and portfolio choices.

- Resilience and stress testing: Climate risks embedded in bank-wide 5-year adverse stress tests using models and expert input; environmental risks to be further integrated. Adverse scenario features abrupt policy tightening, rapid carbon price increases, higher energy prices and inflation, weaker confidence, higher rates/spreads, and falling real estate prices—especially for less energy-efficient properties—leading to a significant GDP hit.

nodes.title: Resilience of our business model to CER risks
nodes.heading: 7.3.18 Resilience of our business model to CER risks

- Environmental risk: Encompasses physical and transition-related environmental degradation impacts on clients and the bank. High-probability, potentially material events relate mainly to regulatory or technological transition factors. Managed through medium/long-term portfolio choices and long-term value creation assessments.

nodes.title: Adverse case scenario
nodes.heading: 7.3.19 Adverse case scenario
nodes.start_phrase: Our adverse macroeconomic scenario assumed an abrupt tightening of climate policies, for instance due to a large physical risk event (not specific to the Netherlands) or lagging targets.
nodes.summary:

- Climate transition risk: Defined as risks from the shift to a lower‑carbon economy via regulation, business model changes, and consumer preference shifts. Assessed as not material in the short term; potentially material in the medium to long term due to regulatory-driven adjustments and policy changes to reduce CER or portfolio emissions.
- Environmental risk: Arises from environmental degradation and the transition to a more sustainable economy, affecting clients and the bank similarly to climate risks. High‑probability, potentially material events linked to regulatory and technological transition factors. Managed through medium/long‑term portfolio choices and strategy, guided by long‑term value creation and impact assessments.
- Resilience and stress testing: Climate risks incorporated into the bank’s 5‑year adverse stress testing; environmental risks to be integrated in future iterations. Methodology combines quantitative models and expert judgment; scope is bank‑wide and aligned with the five‑year financial plan that includes CER effects.
- Adverse scenario: Assumes abrupt tightening of climate policies (e.g., after a major physical event or missed targets). Household incomes and corporate profits are squeezed; higher policy rates and credit spreads dampen demand. Real estate prices fall, with additional Dutch rules penalizing less energy‑efficient buildings, further depressing their values. Overall, a significant hit to real GDP growth is assumed.

nodes.title: Adverse stress test results
nodes.heading: 7.3.20 Adverse stress test results
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the DMA, the bank determined that climate-related and environmental risks are highly likely to materialise over the medium to long term.
nodes.summary:
- The bank’s ICAAP adverse stress test indicates climate and environmental risks (CER) and other risks over a five-year horizon are within loss‑absorbing capacity, confirming the business model’s resilience.
- Climate and ESG are embedded in strategy: commitments to the Paris Agreement and the Net‑Zero Banking Alliance, a climate strategy, and broader social impact initiatives; in mortgages, lending is not discriminated by physical risk indicators due to the bank’s social role.
- Non‑Financial Risk (NFR) materiality assessment methodology evaluates CER-related NFR events over 1-, 5-, and 30‑year horizons, using integrated first- and second-line expert input and updated scenarios.
- Five NFR scenarios assessed: one physical (data centre failure from flooding), three transition/greenwashing (misreporting, mis‑selling, mis‑advertising), and one duty‑of‑care scenario for mortgages (collateral value decline).
- Outcomes: climate physical and transition risks, and environmental transition risks, are material at all time horizons.
- Risk responses:
  - Greenwashing scenarios remain material; response is monitoring with no immediate additional mitigants.
  - Data centre flooding risk could be material within one year; response is monitoring while impacts are investigated.
  - Mortgage duty‑of‑care (physical risk to collateral values) remains material; response is monitoring with no short‑term new mitigants.
- Triggers for action arise from ongoing risk dialogues and major CER‑related events, per NFR policy.
- Social and governance risk materiality is covered via the bank’s double materiality assessment.
- Client sustainability due diligence: during onboarding and periodically, corporate clients are assessed against minimum sustainability standards and generic principles, alongside AML/CFT controls.

nodes.title: Transition Readiness Assessment
nodes.heading: 7.3.27 Transition Readiness Assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The Transition Readiness Assessment (TRA) tool is an engagement instrument used by the first line of defence to evaluate the willingness and ability of corporate clients active in sectors in scope of our climate strategy to adapt to a low-carbon business model (inside-out).
nodes.summary:
- The bank embeds sustainability into client interactions, including sustainable home financing discussions for retail and corporate clients, to safeguard proper business conduct.
- Overview of tools used to assess corporate clients’ sustainability risks:
  - Transition Readiness Assessment (TRA): a first line of defence engagement tool for sectors in scope of the climate strategy, assessing (1) climate performance versus benchmarks and sensitivity to climate risk, (2) ambition and robustness of the client’s CO2 transition plan (targets, governance, monitoring), and (3) ABN AMRO’s ability to support the client’s transition. The second line will consider integrating TRA into credit risk management.
  - Client Assessment on Sustainability (CASY): applied at onboarding and periodic reviews for lending relationships above EUR 1 million; stores key sustainability data, evaluates compliance with the bank’s sustainability risk framework (regulation, commitments, risk management capacity, track record), and rates clients above/on/below par to guide engagement and manage sustainability and reputational risks.
  - CER Risk Classification Tool (RCT): classifies non-programme lending clients by exposure to climate, transition, and environmental (CER) risks; integrates these into creditworthiness at origination and review; assigns risk profiles from low to high and enables data reuse across the credit risk process.
- Transmission Channel Framework (TCF): maps how physical and transition climate factors translate into financial risks via impacts on clients (e.g., productivity losses, asset damage, higher transition costs, obsolescence, property value declines), affecting client creditworthiness and the bank’s P&L.
- The bank enhanced transmission channel assessments for sectors deemed to contribute highly to climate change: Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing; Extraction, Oil & Gas; Manufacturing (Metals & Chemicals); New Energies (Power); Construction; and Shipping, Air & Road transport (with NACE codes used as proxies).

nodes.title: CASY
nodes.heading: 7.3.28 CASY

- CER Risk Classification Tool (RCT): Classifies non‑programme lending clients by exposure to climate, environmental, and transition risks, embedding these in creditworthiness assessments at origination and review. Outputs low–high CER risk profiles and enables data reuse across the credit risk process.
- Transmission Channel Framework (TCF): Describes how physical (e.g., floods, droughts) and transition risks (e.g., higher costs, obsolescence, property value declines for low energy labels) translate into financial impacts on clients, creditworthiness, and the bank’s P&L. nodes.title: Transmission channel framework
nodes.heading: 7.3.30 Transmission channel framework
nodes.start_phrase: Transmission channels are the causal chains through which climate factors translate into financial risks to ABN AMRO by directly influencing our counterparties and the assets they hold.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on integrating sustainability into client dialogues and credit processes, including offering sustainable home financing and continuously safeguarding proper business conduct.
- Overview of tools used to assess sustainability risks for corporate clients:
  - Transition Readiness Assessment (TRA): first-line engagement tool evaluating clients’ climate performance, transition plans, and ABN AMRO’s ability to support; potential integration into the credit risk process by the second line.
  - Client Assessment on Sustainability (CASY): assessment at onboarding and periodic reviews for lending clients > EUR 1 million, capturing compliance with the bank’s sustainability risk framework and rating outcomes (above/on/below par) to guide further engagement.
  - CER Risk Classification Tool (RCT): classifies non-programme lending clients by physical climate, transition, and environmental risk exposure; integrates CER risk into origination and review creditworthiness assessments and enables data reuse within credit risk.
  - Transmission Channel Framework (TCF): maps how physical and transition risks translate into financial impacts and client creditworthiness; enhanced assessments for high-emitting sectors (agriculture/forestry/fishing, extraction/oil & gas, manufacturing metals & chemicals, power/new energies, construction, shipping/air/road transport, real estate); early-stage incorporation into credit proposals.
- Credit Risk Sustainability (second line of defence) governance and escalation:
  - Oversees due diligence and engagement for lending and non-lending clients; provides KYC sustainability risk advice triggered by adverse media, defence-related activities, and potential breaches of the Exclusion or Controversial Weapons lists.
  - For high-risk lending clients with exposure > EUR 1 million, second-line validation is required; clients may be accepted with conditions if committed to compliance, monitored annually; persistent non-compliance can lead to negative advice and potential relationship exit as a last resort. Non-compliance is treated as a credit risk driver.
- Governance of sustainability matters:
  - Executive Board defines strategy and ensures sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities are addressed across the bank.
  - Supervisory Board oversees and advises on sustainability policies and general affairs.
  - Board committees support governance with defined mandates and procedural rules; reference to broader composition and diversity details in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Our approach
nodes.heading: 7.5.1.4 Our approach
nodes.start_phrase: We have set emission reduction targets and ambitions across our lending portfolios, operational activities and client asset portfolios, with a focus on responsibly reducing carbon intensity.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines ABN AMRO’s climate target-setting across lending, operations, and client asset portfolios, focused on responsibly reducing carbon intensity.
- Target-setting is internal (no external stakeholders) and not independently validated; relies on assumptions such as emerging technologies and consumer demand shifts.
- Lending portfolio targets built on three pillars: alignment with industry guidance (NZBA, PCAF), a science-based approach consistent with NZBA, and a sector-based focus prioritizing carbon‑intensive sectors.
- For assets under management, the ISS framework guides measurement; the objective is to reduce clients’ portfolio WACI, especially within equity holdings of DPM mandates.
- Client engagement is a core lever for decarbonisation, with activities tied to risk assessment, measurement, and response.
- Sector materiality is defined by exposure; sectors with drawn exposure below 0.25% of the corporate loan book are deemed immaterial.

- Client engagement is central to the transition strategy, embedded in risk assessment, measurement, and response processes.
- Materiality is defined by exposure: sectors with drawn exposure below 0.25% of the corporate loan book are deemed immaterial.
