nodes.title: Climate scenario analysis, scenario choice and data
nodes.heading: 7.5.1.7.3 Climate scenario analysis, scenario choice and data
nodes.start_phrase: Our loans are concentrated in the Netherlands.
nodes.summary:
- Strategic context and targets: The bank aims to align with Fit for 55 and NZBA pathways. Agricultural exposures represent 2% of total NZBA sector exposure. The scenario used for client assets is not yet science-based. Full 1.5°C alignment is not expected by 2030 for residential mortgages, inland shipping, and road transport trucks/vans; interim targets in these areas are above benchmark trajectories. 2024 marked the second year of the climate strategy and a transition to a refinement phase, updating targets with new data, insights, and methodologies.

- Climate risk governance and monitoring: Climate change is treated as a material sustainability risk embedded in the risk taxonomy and appetite. The bank periodically measures and monitors climate risk exposure and assesses portfolio alignment with its strategy.

- Climate risk heatmap: Sectoral sensitivity to physical and transition risks and negative impacts is assessed. Physical risk inputs use CAS (Netherlands, 2050) and Encore, plus Moody’s ESG Solutions for other geographies (2040); both assume a high-emissions RCP 8.5 scenario. Transition risk uses GHG intensity (PCAF, ISS Oekom) and regulatory parameters from the Dutch Climate Agreement (to 2030) and the Environmental Performance Index. Sectors with highest sensitivities: agriculture (NACE A), mining (B), manufacturing (C), power generation (D), and transport (H).

- Scenario analysis and data coverage: With lending concentrated in the Netherlands, material physical risk lies in Dutch regions (NUTS). Physical risk assessment covers corporate loans, residential mortgages, and commercial real estate, representing 96% of collateralised loans. In 2024, long-term (to 2050) scenario analyses for residential and commercial real estate assessed physical risks (floods, foundation issues, wildfires, heat stress) and transition risks, incorporating adaptation plans. Flood assumptions follow RCP 8.5 (approx. 4.3°C by 2100). Vulnerable customers are those with high LTV/LTI and/or Stage 2 risk; vulnerable collateral has energy label D or worse and value ≤ EUR 300,000. Impacts on creditworthiness feed into RWA and provision calculations and CER materiality for Credit and Liquidity risks.

- Data sources and methodologies: Foundation risk data from KCAF; other physical hazards from CAS with granular Dutch data. CAS uses KNMI’14 WH scenarios to 2050 and KNMI’23 for flood risk, aligned with NGFS current policies scenario. Results are presented as risk distributions for CRE and RRE across foundation, flood, wildfire, and heat stress, with probabilities bucketed from no risk to high risk (plus no data).

- Risk mitigation: Climate risk is addressed through established risk response processes within overall sustainability risk management.

Cumulative deployed is EUR 333 million since 2022, including EUR 31 million in direct equity and EUR 49 million in fund allocations in 2024. Investments are channeled via direct equity (Sustainable Impact Fund focused on energy transition, built environment, sustainable consumption), climate-focused third-party funds (SFDR Article 8/9), and hybrid debt. Progress is monitored quarterly and mapped to financial statement items (Other equity associates within Equity accounted investments and Financial investments).

nodes.title: Business conduct (Governance)
nodes.heading: 7.7 Business conduct (Governance)
nodes.start_phrase: We are subject to strict regulatory requirements, at both national and international level.
nodes.summary:

- Materiality assessment identifies Client Integrity as a material topic, with vigilance required to safeguard the banking system.

  - Client Acceptance and Anti-Money Laundering (CAAML) Policy: measures to prevent/detect ML/FT and manage associated risks.

  - Fraud Risk Policy: minimum standards for managing fraud risk (including first-party fraud) through prevention, detection and response; adaptive to evolving fraud threats.
  - Sanctions Policy: rules to prevent prohibited transactions and sanctions evasion, with requirements, consequences, escalation and reporting.
- Policies collectively reinforce legal compliance (e.g., Dutch Financial Supervision Act, AML/CTF Act, Sanctions Act 1977), industry best practices and positive culture to mitigate financial crime.
- All policies are accessible on the bank’s intranet; an AML, CTF and Sanctions Statement and the ABC Policy are publicly available.

nodes.title: Client integrity
nodes.heading: 7.7.1 Client integrity
nodes.start_phrase: Client Integrity risk at ABN AMRO encompasses six key risk types: Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Bribery and Corruption, Combating the Financing of Terrorism, Tax, Fraud and Sanctions.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of business conduct and governance: the bank operates under strict national and international regulations, translated into internal policies with monitoring mechanisms to ensure operational effectiveness, compliance, risk awareness, and a culture of integrity.
- Materiality: Client Integrity is identified as a material topic (financial materiality per DMA). Key stakeholders include clients, regulators, employees, shareholders, and society.
- Client Integrity risk scope: six risk types—Anti-Money Laundering (AML), Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC), Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT), Tax, Fraud, and Sanctions.
- Policy framework:
  - Client Acceptance and Anti-Money Laundering (CAAML) Policy: sets measures to prevent/detect ML/FT and manage related risks.
  - Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC) Policy: addresses bribery/corruption risks across clients, employees, the organization, and third parties; includes risk indicators (e.g., adverse media).
  - Tax Policy: defines global tax mandate, responsible tax behavior, strategy, risk appetite, and control framework.
  - Fraud Risk Policy: establishes standards for preventing, detecting, and responding to fraud (including first-party fraud) within an adaptive framework.
  - Sanctions Policy: prevents prohibited/sanctions-evasive transactions; outlines rules, consequences, escalation, and reporting.
- Policy governance: policies apply globally to all entities; stricter local laws prevail. ABC Policy also covers employees and third parties. Policies are on the intranet; AML/CTF/Sanctions statement and ABC Policy are publicly available. Policy adherence and key controls are periodically monitored and tested.
- Training: employees are required to understand AML/CFT responsibilities; a dedicated Client Integrity training curriculum and ongoing training are provided.

The Dutch Central Bank is monitoring progress and has identified shortcomings in event-driven reviews (updating client files), which may lead to enforcement; financial impact is uncertain and no provision has been recorded.
- Broader bribery and corruption stance: the bank works to strengthen internal policies, processes, and controls for employees and third parties; further details in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Governance risks with counterparties and clients: managed via non-financial risk management (fraud, third-party, outsourcing) and client sustainability assessments; related disclosures referenced elsewhere.

nodes.title: Financed GHG emissions
nodes.heading: 7.8.2 Financed GHG emissions
nodes.start_phrase: The financed GHG emissions have been calculated according to the Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard for the Financial Industry (PCAF, December 2022).
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines how financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are calculated in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (December 2022), allocating emissions proportionally to the bank’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s value.
- It prioritizes client- or collateral-level data; where unavailable, it applies economic emission intensities relevant to each segment.
- It summarizes portfolio-specific data sources and methods:
  - Corporate loans (listed bonds and equity): ISS ESG and client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed NL): Statistics Netherlands (CBS) economic intensity.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed RoW): PCAF emission factor database.
  - Agriculture: sector-specific factor for dairy (RVO, International Dairy Federation, Hospers et al. 2022); CBS intensities for other subsectors.
  - Shipping: Poseidon Principles and third parties (e.g., DNV) and emissiefactoren.nl/KiM; client-reported for sea/coastal freight; intensities for inland and other subsectors; CBS/PCAF as fallback.
  - Oil and gas (upstream/midstream): Rystad Energy, company disclosures, IPCC factors; specific emissions via Rystad.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch government open data; client-reported emissions and average capacity factor estimates.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft emission factors by vehicle type.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF database; estimates by building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; estimates by building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Additional methodological notes:
  - For corporate clients not in ISS ESG, CBS and PCAF provide country/sector carbon intensities.
  - Renewable energy producers (solar, wind, hydro) are assigned zero scope 1 and 2 emissions; scope 3 uses client data or CBS/PCAF.
  - Shipping data are collected and validated at vessel level under Poseidon Principles; inland shipping uses external emission factors; CBS/PCAF used when gaps exist.
  - Oil and gas intensity metric is kg CO2e per barrel produced/distributed/transported; client disclosures are linked with Rystad production and intensity data to set baselines and targets.

nodes.title: ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
nodes.heading: 7.9 ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
nodes.start_phrase: Specifically for loans collateralised by residential immovable property, the amounts attributed to EPC labels in this report consist of EPC labels under the old regulation (NEN7120, prior to 1 January 2021) and new regulation (NTA8800) as provided by Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland (RVO).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: ESG2 disclosure on climate change transition risk for ABN AMRO’s banking book, focusing on the energy efficiency of collateral for loans secured by immovable property (residential and commercial) using EP scores (kWh/m²) and EPC labels.
- Methodology and data sources:
  - Residential EPC labels include both old regulation (NEN7120, pre-2021) and new regulation (NTA8800) as provided by RVO.
  - Only the new regulation EP score is “official” in EP score columns; old-regulation EP scores are treated as estimated.
  - EP score columns (B–G) combine official and estimated values; EPC label columns (H–N) include only official labels.
  - Exposures without an official EPC label are reported under “Without EPC label of collateral,” including buildings exempt from labels (e.g., monuments), assets under development/not yet registered, and cases where the label is unknown to the bank.
- Portfolio strategy and progress:
  - ABN AMRO targets lower portfolio emissions by increasing A and higher-than-A labels and reducing exposure to D–G labels.
  - From 30 June 2024 to 31 December 2024, official energy labels increased from 52% to 55%; 76% of the portfolio had a label of C or higher (vs 74% on 30 June 2024).
  - Growth in A and higher-than-A driven by new inflow (labels mandatory at sale/purchase) and migration from lower-than-A; new-build homes under the Building Decree have at least A+++.

  - Sector sensitivities to physical risk (NACE level 4 via the Environmental and Social Risk Heatmap), with examples such as flood sensitivity driven by reliance on physical assets and water stress sensitivity based on water dependence.
- Details data sources by geography/asset type and hazard:
  - Netherlands, residential real estate collateral: Climate Impact Atlas (flooding, wildfires) and Kennis Centrum Aanpak Funderingsproblematiek (foundation risks).
  - Netherlands, other loans/collateral: CIA (flooding) and Moody’s ESG Solutions (wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes/typhoons, sea level rise).
  - Outside the Netherlands: Moody’s ESG Solutions (flooding, wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes/typhoons, sea level rise).
  - Notes foundation problems as a key driver of physical climate risk in Dutch real estate.
- Describes exposure classification:
  - Starts from climate hazard exposure at the counterparty’s or collateral’s location.
  - Marks sensitivity to acute/chronic risk per Moody’s ESG Solutions methodology if sensitive to any underlying hazard.
  - Uses an alternative Dutch flooding rule: classify as acute-risk sensitive if at least 10% of buildings in the NUTS region face >0.5 m flooding.
- Presents ESG6 summary of EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs and coverage:
  - 31 Dec 2024: GAR stock—Climate change mitigation 11%, adaptation 0%, total 11%; KPI coverage over total assets 80%. Flow coverage not feasible because total assets for flow are not in the template.
  - 30 Jun 2024: GAR stock—mitigation 9%, adaptation 0%, total 9%; KPI coverage 81%. Flow figures left blank; reporting to start Q4 2024 to align with the Integrated Annual Report. Coverage change driven by updated formula and guidance (now comparing covered assets to total assets).
  - 31 Dec 2023: GAR stock—mitigation 10%, adaptation 0%, total 10%; KPI coverage 8%.
- Provides ESG7 information on assets used for GAR calculation (31 Dec 2024 reference date):
  - Lists covered assets included in both numerator and denominator (loans and advances, debt securities, equity instruments not held for trading).
  - Breaks down exposures by counterparty type (e.g., financial corporations, credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings, non-financial corporations subject to NFRD), and by instrument.
  - Shows taxonomy relevance and alignment for Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation, including flags for specialised lending and transitional/enabling/adaptation categories.

- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures from ABN AMRO’s Pillar 3 Report 2024, covering KPI scope, methodology, and detailed breakdowns for 31 Dec 2023, 30 Jun 2024, and 31 Dec 2024.
- KPI coverage and timing:
  - KPI% coverage over total assets (Dec-2023) shows circa 10% coverage for climate change mitigation; climate adaptation coverage was 0% at that time.
  - GAR “flow” metrics are left blank; reporting will start from Q4 2024 to align with the Integrated Annual Report 2024 approach.
- GAR composition and methodology:
  - Detailed allocation of assets between numerator and denominator per EU Taxonomy rules, with explicit categories:
    - Included in numerator and denominator: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds), and equity not held for trading.
    - Excluded from numerator but included in denominator: EU and non-EU non-financial corporates not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, cash, and other assets.
    - Excluded from both numerator and denominator: sovereigns, central bank exposures, and trading book positions.
  - Reconciliation note: Because the Pillar 3 template lacks a line for non-NFRD financial corporations, these are shown under “other assets” to reconcile FINREP and EU Taxonomy definitions.
- Asset class breakdowns:
  - Financial corporations: split into credit institutions, other financial corporations (including investment firms and management companies), and insurance undertakings; instruments split into loans, debt securities (incl. UoP), and equity.
  - Non-financial corporations subject to NFRD: reported with taxonomy-eligible and aligned amounts.
  - Households: major share of GAR assets, driven by mortgages (loans collateralised by residential property), renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans; collateral obtained by possession is also shown.
- Climate objectives and sub-categories:
  - Both Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) are reported, including “specialised lending,” “transitional,” and “enabling” categories where applicable.
- Key quantitative highlights (illustrative from the period tables):
  - Total assets and GAR denominators:
    - Dec-2023: total assets ~390bn; GAR denominator ~305bn (with ~85bn excluded: sovereigns, central banks, trading).
    - Jun-2024: total assets ~406bn; GAR denominator ~328bn (with ~78bn excluded).
    - Dec-2024: total assets ~395bn; GAR denominator ~315bn (with ~79bn excluded).
  - Households dominate GAR-covered assets; mortgages represent the bulk (circa 155–158bn across periods).
  - Taxonomy eligibility and alignment (Dec-2024 ESG8 KPIs on stock):
    - Within covered assets: CCM-eligible ≈ 52%, of which ≈ 11% aligned; CCA-eligible ≈ 50%.
    - Households: 100% CCM-eligible; a material portion (about 22%) is CCM-aligned; household mortgages and renovation loans are now also assessed under CCA.
- Methodological updates and clarifications:
  - Household activities: CCM eligibility is used as the primary measure to capture all household-related eligibility (including items that would also be eligible under CCA and Circular Economy) to avoid double counting.
  - Regulatory update: building renovation loans and loans collateralised by residential property are newly included under CCA in 2024 due to EU Taxonomy scope expansion.

- Purpose and scope: The excerpt presents ABN AMRO’s EU Taxonomy-aligned Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures (ESG8) and a supplementary disclosure on other climate-mitigating actions (ESG10) from the Pillar 3 Report 2024. It covers key performance indicators (KPIs) on both stock and flow bases for Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) across multiple reporting dates (31 Dec 2023, 30 Jun 2024, 31 Dec 2024).

- GAR KPIs on stock:
  - Measures the proportion of eligible assets funding taxonomy-relevant sectors and, within that, the share that is environmentally sustainable.
  - Breakdowns by counterparty segments: financial corporations (including credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial corporations subject to NFRD, households (with sub-categories: mortgages collateralised by residential property, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral obtained.
  - Additional splits by lending type: specialised lending, transitional (for CCM), enabling activities, and for CCA: specialised lending, adaptation, enabling.
  - Headline pattern: overall eligibility is roughly stable around 49–52% across dates, with environmentally sustainable shares around 9–11% at the aggregate level; households are consistently shown as 100% eligible with circa 20–22% environmentally sustainable shares, and mortgages mirror this; building renovation loans are shown as fully eligible/sustainable within households.

- GAR KPIs on flows:
  - For 31 Dec 2023 and 30 Jun 2024, flow fields are intentionally left blank; flow reporting starts in Q4 2024 to align with the Integrated Annual Report 2024 approach.
  - As of 31 Dec 2024, flow KPIs show high coverage of new assets (generally around mid-90s to 100%), with environmentally sustainable shares around the low-20s overall; household flows show high coverage and circa 24% sustainable; non-financial corporates and financial corporates present segment-specific coverage and sustainable shares; enabling, transitional/adaptation, and specialised lending splits are provided.

- Methodological and scope notes:
  - Alignment challenge between FINREP and EU Taxonomy: exposures towards non-NFRD financial corporations are placed in “other assets” in the P3 template to reconcile with EU Taxonomy disclosures; totals for “Other financial corporations” account for entities considered financial in FINREP but non-financial under the EU Taxonomy.
  - Household methodology: CCM eligibility is used as the primary measure to capture the full household-related eligibility scope (also covering CCA and Circular Economy) and to avoid double counting.
  - Regulatory update impact: in 2024, household loans collateralised by residential property and renovation loans are included under CCA, reflecting the EU Taxonomy update expanding these products beyond CCM to CCA.

- ESG10 – Other climate change mitigating actions not covered by the EU Taxonomy:
  - Presents exposures that support climate mitigation but do not meet the EU Taxonomy’s strict technical screening criteria or scope.
  - Based on ABN AMRO’s Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS), aligned with market practice and SFDR; a climate-focused subset of SAS-labelled “acceleration” loans is reported (e.g., clean transportation, sustainable real estate).
  - Exposures increased by year-end 2024 versus mid-2024, mainly due to new mortgage production.
  - Notes that only a limited portion of exposures are EU Taxonomy-aligned given its narrow scope and strict criteria; hence, most climate-mitigating exposures appear in this non-Taxonomy template.

nodes.start_phrase: This template includes other climate change mitigating actions that are not aligned with the strict criteria of the EU Taxonomy, but nevertheless support counterparties in mitigating climate change related risks.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents ESG10 exposures—other climate change–mitigating actions not meeting the strict EU Taxonomy criteria but supporting clients in managing climate-related risks. The bank uses a subset of its internal Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS), aligned with EU SFDR and market practice, filtered to climate-focused categories (e.g., clean transport, sustainable real estate).
- EU Taxonomy alignment: Only a limited share is EU Taxonomy–aligned due to the Technical Screening Criteria, limited scope (including NFRD), and other strict requirements; therefore, most exposures are reported in this Pillar 3 ESG10 template.
- Risk coverage: Actions primarily mitigate climate transition risk. Physical risk mitigation is flagged mainly for green bonds; loans are reported as mitigating transition risk, not physical risk.
- Instruments and counterparties:
  - Bonds: Green bonds from European banks and sovereigns/government-guaranteed issuers (Austria, Germany, Finland, France, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Philippines, Sweden, EU; Denmark noted in 2023). Use-of-proceeds frameworks cover both mitigation and adaptation.
  - Loans: Financing internally classified as sustainable under SAS with a climate mitigation purpose. Counterparties include financial corporations, non-financial corporations (with a material share collateralised by commercial real estate), and households (predominantly residential mortgages; no separate building renovation loans reported).
- Reported balances (gross carrying amounts, in millions) at 31 Dec 2024:
  - Bonds: Financial corporations ~439; Other counterparties (sovereign/guaranteed) ~1,910.
  - Loans: Financial corporations ~1,665; Non-financial corporations ~14,329 (of which commercial real estate ~5,317); Households ~16,508 (of which residential mortgages ~15,278).
- Time-series context (31 Dec 2023, 30 Jun 2024, 31 Dec 2024): Balances are shown for three dates, with category-level movements over time. The narrative notes higher exposures at 31 Dec 2024 versus 30 Jun 2024, driven mainly by inflows from new mortgage production. Financial- and non-financial-corporate sustainable loans generally trend up across the period; sovereign/guaranteed green bond holdings fluctuate; building renovation loans remain unreported.
- Standards note: Instruments include green, sustainable, and sustainability-linked types under standards other than EU standards.
